calculator.metaTitle: Fertilizer Dose Calculator — Urea, DAP & MOP per Acre/Kanal/Marla
calculator.metaDescription: Calculate exact urea, DAP and MOP doses per acre, kanal, marla or hectare — see how many 50 kg bags you need for wheat, rice, maize and more crops.

methodFaq.a: Phosphorus is immobile in soil, so the full P₂O₅ dose must come from DAP at sowing. DAP also contains 18% nitrogen, which counts toward the total nitrogen need — calculating DAP first lets us subtract that nitrogen before computing urea, so you never double-dose nitrogen.

methodFaq.q: How many bags of urea do I need per acre?
methodFaq.a: It depends on your crop's nitrogen requirement. For example, wheat needs 124 kg N per hectare (≈50 kg N per acre). Since urea contains 46% nitrogen, that's about 109 kg of urea per acre — roughly 2.2 bags of 50 kg each. Select your crop above and the calculator shows the exact bag count for your area.

methodFaq.q: How many bags of DAP do I need per acre?
methodFaq.a: DAP contains 18% nitrogen and 46% P₂O₅. For wheat (62 kg P₂O₅ per hectare ≈ 25 kg per acre), you need about 55 kg of DAP per acre — just over 1 bag of 50 kg. The calculator above computes the precise amount including the nitrogen bonus DAP provides.

methodFaq.q: How are kanal and marla converted?
methodFaq.a: 1 acre = 8 kanal = 160 marla, and 1 kanal = 20 marla. In metric: 1 acre = 0.4047 ha, 1 kanal = 0.0506 ha, 1 marla = 0.00253 ha. The calculator converts your area to hectares, applies the per-hectare dose, then scales back.

A crop is only selectable when its recommended NPK dose is verified against a published source. We would rather disable a crop than invent its figures — unverified crops are marked "data in review" until confirmed.

organic.warnTitle: Read this before trusting the numbers
organic.warnBody: Organic materials vary batch to batch — feedstock, preparation and storage change the analysis. Published ranges are not your batch's analysis. Organic nitrogen also releases slowly (only ~30% of FYM nitrogen is available to the first crop, per TNAU), so treat the result as nutrients applied, not nutrients available this season. For precision, get a lab analysis of your actual material.

items.a: With the standard agronomic formula: fertilizer (kg) = (nutrient needed × 100) ÷ nutrient % in the fertilizer. We apply it DAP-first — phosphorus from DAP, then the remaining nitrogen from urea (accounting for DAP's 18% nitrogen), then potassium from MOP — and show every step.
items.q: How is the fertilizer dose calculated?

items.a: Acre, kanal, marla and hectare. Conversions used: 1 acre = 8 kanal = 160 marla, 1 kanal = 20 marla, 1 hectare = 2.471 acres.

Published provincial and research-institute recommendations (e.g. PAU package of practices), region-tagged. Every figure in the calculator carries its source citation, and crops without a verified source are marked 'data in review' rather than guessed.
items.q: Where do the crop nutrient figures come from?

items.a: No. It gives AI-assisted possibilities with uncertainty wording, but you should always confirm with your local agriculture officer before treating a crop — especially before spraying anything.
items.q: Is the Plant Doctor a replacement for an agronomist?

items.a: Yes — the calculator, libraries and guides are free. An account is only needed for features like saving diagnoses.
items.q: Is Fertilizer Dose free to use?
Can I mix urea and DAP together?
items.a: Yes, urea and DAP can be applied together as a basal dose at sowing. DAP provides phosphorus (46% P₂O₅) plus 18% nitrogen, while urea adds more nitrogen (46% N). A common practice is to mix them before broadcasting. However, avoid mixing urea with SSP (single super phosphate) in the same application if the mixture will sit — it can become lumpy. Always check your crop's recommended NPK ratio first.

items.q: What is basal dose in fertilizer?
items.a: The basal dose is the fertilizer applied at or before sowing/planting, worked into the soil. It typically includes the full phosphorus and potassium requirement plus a portion of nitrogen (usually 1/3 to 1/2). The remaining nitrogen is given as top-dressing later — for example, urea at tillering for wheat. Basal application ensures nutrients are available to young roots from day one.

items.q: DAP vs SSP — which is better?
items.a: It depends on your soil and crop. DAP (18-46-0) has higher phosphorus concentration (46% P₂O₅), so you need less product per acre — good for transport and handling. SSP (16% P₂O₅) also provides sulphur (~11%) and calcium (~19%), making it better for oilseeds, pulses, and sulphur-deficient soils. DAP is usually cheaper per kg of phosphorus, but SSP adds secondary nutrients. Use our Compare tool to check which is cheaper per kg of P₂O₅ at your local prices.

items.q: What is soil test based fertilizer dose?
items.a: A soil test measures your soil's existing nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, pH, and organic matter. Instead of using a blanket recommendation, the fertilizer dose is adjusted — if your soil already has high phosphorus, you apply less P fertilizer. This saves money and prevents over-fertilization. We recommend getting a soil test every 2-3 years through your local agriculture department. Our calculator uses standard recommendations; for soil-test-based precision doses, consult your local soil testing lab with these standard figures as a starting point.

method.title: The method, in plain words
method.desc: Build-up, maintenance, drawdown — the same logic soil labs use on health cards.

methodFaq.q: What is a soil test based fertilizer dose?
methodFaq.a: A blanket recommendation assumes an average soil. A soil test tells you what your field already holds: if phosphorus tests high, you can cut the P dose and save money; if it tests low, you raise it to build the soil up. This tool starts from a verified crop recommendation and applies exactly that logic — +30% for low-rated nutrients, base for medium, −25% for high.

methodFaq.q: Which soil-test values do I need?
methodFaq.a: Available phosphorus (Olsen method, mg/kg or ppm), available potassium (ammonium acetate method, kg/ha or ppm), organic carbon (%), and pH — the four values on a standard soil health card. You can enter P and K in either unit; the tool converts with the standard furrow-slice factor (×2.24).

methodFaq.q: Why is nitrogen rated from organic carbon?
methodFaq.a: Routine soil labs rarely report a mineral-nitrogen class, so extension systems use organic carbon as the proxy for native nitrogen-supplying capacity: more organic carbon means more nitrogen will mineralize during the season. It is a well-established proxy, but it is not a measured N value — the result is labeled as such.

methodFaq.q: Does an alkaline pH change my dose?
methodFaq.a: No — pH never changes the calculated dose here. Above pH 7.5, phosphorus increasingly precipitates as calcium and magnesium phosphates (P fixation), so placement matters: band the full phosphorus dose near the seed at sowing instead of broadcasting. The tool flags this as a note, not a dose change.

methodFaq.q: When should I not use the custom base dose?
methodFaq.a: The custom base option is generic guidance only — a starting point for crops with no verified recommendation in our database. If a verified crop×region dose exists, always use that instead; verified figures carry their published source.

organic.metaTitle: Organic Fertilizers — Types, Nutrient Ranges & Honest Limitations
organic.metaDescription: Farmyard manure, compost, vermicompost and green manure: typical NPK ranges from extension sources, how organics differ from mineral fertilizers, and their real limitations.
organic.title: Slow, variable — and honest about it.
organic.intro: Organic fertilizers are plant and animal wastes that release nutrients as they decompose. They build soil, but they are dilute and inconsistent compared with mineral fertilizers. This page gives you typical nutrient ranges from published extension sources, and the limitations nobody should skip.
organic.whatBody1: Manures are plant and animal wastes used as sources of plant nutrients; they release those nutrients after decomposition (TNAU). The most widely used bulky organic manures are farmyard manure (FYM), compost and green manure. A second group — concentrated organic manures such as oilcakes, blood meal and bone meal — carries more nutrients per kilogram but is still far below mineral concentrations.
organic.whatBody2: The defining trait of organics is variability: the same material from two farms can differ several-fold in nutrient content depending on feedstock, preparation and storage. That is why this library shows ranges, never single label values, for organic materials.
organic.typesTitle: The four materials in this library
organic.typesIntro: Each card shows the typical N–P₂O₅–K₂O percentage range from published extension sources. Your batch will differ — these are starting points, not guarantees.
organic.compareTitle: How organics differ from mineral fertilizers
organic.compareIntro: Neither side is 'always better'. They do different jobs:

compareRows.mineral: High and exact — urea is 46% N, printed on the bag.
compareRows.organic: Low and variable — FYM is roughly 0.5–1.0% N, and every heap differs.

compareRows.mineral: Fast — nutrients are water-soluble and available within days.
compareRows.organic: Slow — microbes must mineralize them first; only ~30% of FYM nitrogen reaches the first crop (TNAU).

compareRows.mineral: Precise — the calculator can dose to the kilogram.
compareRows.organic: Approximate without a lab analysis of your specific batch.

compareRows.mineral: Little direct effect on soil structure or organic matter.
compareRows.organic: Improves structure, water-holding capacity and microbial activity.

compareRows.mineral: Concentrated — a few bags per acre.
compareRows.organic: Bulky — tonnes per hectare to move, spread and incorporate.

compareRows.mineral: Mostly taken up or lost within the season.
compareRows.organic: Long — feeds subsequent crops as decomposition continues.

uses: Building soil organic matter and structure over seasons — their strongest role.
Basal soil conditioning before sowing, especially on degraded or sandy soils.
Integrated nutrient management: organics for soil health plus mineral fertilizers for precise crop nutrition.
Nurseries, vegetables and high-value crops where soil biology pays back fastest.
Green manuring before transplanted rice, where dhaincha can add 130–185 kg N/ha of biologically fixed nitrogen.
organic.limitsTitle: Limitations — read before relying on them
limits: Low nutrient density: matching 100 kg N/ha with FYM needs 10–20 tonnes per hectare.
Variable composition: published ranges span 2–3× within a single material; only a lab analysis of your batch is precise.
Slow release: nutrients arrive over months, not days — they cannot rescue a mid-season deficiency.
Bulk and labour: tonnes to transport, spread and incorporate, versus bags of mineral fertilizer.
Quality risks: weed seeds and pathogens in poorly composted material; possible contaminants in municipal compost.
Not a drop-in replacement: 'manure instead of fertilizer' only works as a partial substitution inside a planned nutrient budget — never as an unqualified claim.
organic.warnBody: The calculator's organic section runs pure arithmetic on numbers YOU enter (your lab report or supplier label). It does not know your batch's real analysis, and it cannot account for slow release — treat its output as an upper bound on nutrients applied, not nutrients available to this season's crop. For precision dosing, get a lab analysis of your actual material.
